title: Odile and the Orchard
premise: In 1914, Paloma Vasquez drives for suffragist Odile Marchand along the English coast, reading her mail out of habit and loneliness. When a census taker's probing questions expose that Odile's dearest correspondent is now a German national, Paloma must choose between the loyalty she owes her employer and the truth she owes herself. The two women race to keep a peacetime promise — delivering Odile's final letter to the docks before the last ship sails on the morning tide. They fail to reach it in time, but the letter finds its way years later through Paloma's own hand, teaching her that history was never happening to other people.
about_author: August Almeida is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in coastal county records. Their fiction explores the quiet people standing just outside history's frame.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Reads First
chapters.summary: Paloma Vasquez opens and reads every letter she delivers for suffragist Odile Marchand, telling herself it's diligence. POV: Paloma. Establishes her belief that history happens elsewhere, to other people; the emotional beat is comfortable self-deception.

chapters.title: Letters from Across the Water
chapters.summary: Odile dictates replies to her oldest friend, Greta Lindqvist, a German botanist. Paloma notices the letters avoid politics entirely. POV: Paloma. The beat is tenderness shadowed by something unspoken between the women.

chapters.title: The Orchard at Wren Hollow
chapters.summary: A rare day off: Odile and Paloma walk the abandoned orchard where Odile and Greta once planted trees as students. POV: alternating. Odile reveals fragments of their shared past; Paloma feels, for the first time, that she belongs somewhere.

chapters.title: One Question Too Many
chapters.summary: The census taker arrives. His questions about household members and 'correspondents abroad' linger too long on Greta's name. POV: Paloma. The beat is dread arriving quietly, like weather changing.

chapters.title: War Is Declared Elsewhere
chapters.summary: Britain enters the war. Newspapers shout; the village celebrates. Odile goes silent and burns nothing, which frightens Paloma more than flames would. POV: Odile. The beat is grief wearing a public face.

chapters.title: The Interrogation of Small Things
chapters.summary: A constable visits asking about 'enemy correspondence.' Paloma lies smoothly for the first time in her life and doesn't know who she's protecting anymore. POV: Paloma. The beat is the first crack in loyalty.

chapters.title: What the Letters Never Said
chapters.summary: Paloma rereads four years of letters and realizes they were written in a private code of orchards and seasons. She confronts Odile. POV: Paloma. The beat is betrayal curdling into curiosity.

chapters.title: Greta's Last Letter
chapters.summary: A letter arrives postmarked before the war: Greta is ill, stranded, and asks Odile to keep one promise — plant the seventh tree. POV: Odile. The beat is love made urgent by distance.

chapters.title: The Promise Made in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: 1910, the orchard, young Odile and Greta swearing an oath under the half-planted row. POV: Odile. The beat is warmth that now reads as debt.

chapters.title: Enemy Property
chapters.summary: Authorities seal Greta's confiscated research shipment at the coastal depot; among it, a letter addressed to Odile. Only personal delivery will release it. POV: Paloma. The beat is hope with a deadline attached.

chapters.title: The Ship on the Morning Tide
chapters.summary: The depot clerk mentions the confiscated effects ship out on the morning tide — after that, gone forever. POV: Paloma. The beat is a clock starting inside her chest.

chapters.title: Odile Refuses to Run
chapters.summary: Odile, watched by authorities, cannot travel without confirming suspicion. She orders Paloma not to go. Paloma packs anyway. POV: Odile. The beat is pride cracking into fear for someone else.

chapters.title: The Road to the Coast
chapters.summary: Paloma drives through blackout villages, forged papers borrowed from the suffrage network in the seat beside her. POV: Paloma. The beat is terror transfigured into purpose.

chapters.title: Checkpoint at Marlow Bridge
chapters.summary: A suspicious sergeant questions her story; a stranger — a soldier on leave — vouches for her at cost to himself. POV: Paloma. The beat is discovering strangers can be kind, which undoes her worldview.

chapters.title: The Depot at Night
chapters.summary: Paloma breaks into the sealed warehouse and finds Greta's crates — and learns the letter inside names Odile, not Greta, as its keeper of a secret. POV: Paloma. The beat is truth as a burden she never asked to carry.

chapters.title: What Odile Hid
chapters.summary: The letter reveals Odile passed Greta's pacifist writings through the suffrage network — treasonous now. Delivering it protects Greta but endangers Odile. POV: Paloma. The beat is loyalty and truth pulling in opposite directions.

chapters.title: Caught at the Gate
chapters.summary: Paloma is detained leaving the depot; the letter is nearly discovered. She swallows her fear and lies magnificently. POV: Paloma. The beat is courage she didn't know she owned.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Paloma reaches the quay as the ship casts off. She is seconds late. The crate sails without the letter — she kept it. POV: Paloma. The beat is failure that feels strangely like choice.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Orchard
chapters.summary: Paloma returns and demands everything. Odile confesses all; Paloma must decide whether to report her or keep the secret. POV: alternating. The beat is the rawest honesty either woman has ever spoken.

chapters.title: The Seventh Tree
chapters.summary: Together they plant the seventh tree in frozen ground, keeping the promise the only way left. POV: Odile. The beat is mourning transformed into ritual.

chapters.title: The Years Between
chapters.summary: Epilogue-in-motion: 1919. Greta, surviving, arrives at Wren Hollow; Paloma hands her the letter she has guarded five years. POV: Paloma. The beat is a promise kept late, and completely.

chapters.title: History Happens Here
chapters.summary: Final chapter: Paloma, now running the restored orchard, reads a new letter openly, by daylight, no shame. POV: Paloma. The beat is belonging earned — she was never outside history; she was holding it.
